title: Real-time Gaming Leaderboard
problem: Design a real-time global leaderboard for a mobile game: top-100 worldwide, top-K by region, and a given player's rank with surrounding neighbors, all updated in near real-time.
summary: A read-heavy ranking system built around a Redis Sorted Set (ZSET) as the hot in-memory source of truth for rank, backed by a durable SQL/KV store for history, snapshots, and cold reads. The dominant design choice is using Redis ZSET's skiplist — which gives O(log N) ZADD and O(log N + M) ZREVRANGE — instead of computing ranks from a SQL ORDER BY (which would be O(N log N) per read at 100M rows). The main tradeoff is that Redis is not authoritative storage: scores are persisted asynchronously to the durable DB, and a periodic snapshot job rebuilds the ZSET from the DB to guard against Redis loss. Realtime push via WebSocket is optional but essential for tournament UX — only fire on events that actually change top-K or the player's displayed neighborhood. Sized for ~100M monthly players, ~1M concurrent, ~50K score submissions/sec, ~500K leaderboard reads/sec.

functional: Return the global top-100 leaderboard in ranked order
Return top-K by region, country, or tournament bracket
Return the N players immediately above and below a given player
Accept score submissions and reflect them in the leaderboard within 1 second
Support per-tournament leaderboards with independent lifecycles
nonFunctional: p99 read latency under 50ms for top-K and rank queries
p99 write latency under 100ms for score submissions
At least 99.95% availability on the read path
Durable history of every submitted score for audit and replay
Horizontal scalability by sharded ZSETs (per region or per tournament)
Graceful degradation: reads continue even if the durable DB is unavailable

assumptions: 100M monthly active players, 10M daily, 1M concurrent at peak
Each player submits ~5 scores per session, average session 10 min
Leaderboard is viewed roughly 3x per session (entry screen + post-match + social tab)
Top-100 global + 10 regional boards + 1 per-friend-group board
Score freshness target: < 1 second from submit to visible in leaderboard
estimates: Score writes: 10M * 5 / 86400 ≈ 580 QPS avg, peak ~50K/sec during tournaments
Redis ZSET size: 100M entries * ~80 bytes/entry ≈ 8 GB (fits easily on one node, sharded by region for HA)
Durable DB storage: 10M daily * 5 submissions * 200 bytes * 365 ≈ 3.6 TB/year history
WebSocket fan-out: 1M concurrent * 0.1 actively-viewing ≈ 100K live subscribers during a tournament

architecture.mermaid: graph LR client[Game Client] --> lb[Load Balancer] lb --> ingest[Score Ingest API] lb --> read[Leaderboard Read API] ingest --> zset[(Redis ZSET)] ingest --> db[(Scores DB)] read --> cache[Redis Cache] read --> zset snap[Snapshot Job] --> db snap --> zset ingest --> ws[WebSocket Push]

client.name: Game Client
client.summary: Mobile / console / web game that submits scores after a match and renders leaderboards on the social screens.

sections.heading: Submit path
sections.body: After a match ends, client signs the score (HMAC of match_id + score + client nonce with a session key) and POSTs to /v1/scores. Signing is critical — unsigned scores invite trivial cheating.

sections.heading: Read path
sections.body:
- Top-100 global on the lobby screen
- Top-K by region when user opens the regional tab
- Player's own rank + 5 above / 5 below for the 'where am I?' card
- Optional WebSocket subscription during a live tournament for real-time ticker

sections.heading: Client-side smoothing
sections.body: Clients show the last known leaderboard immediately (from local cache) while issuing a background refresh — perceived latency stays flat even when the server is 100ms away.

bottlenecks.title: Session signing key compromise / client tampering
bottlenecks.trigger: A reverse-engineered game binary on a rooted device extracts the HMAC session key, letting an attacker POST arbitrary scores (e.g. score=2^31-1) to /v1/scores. At 50K ingest QPS, even 0.1% fraudulent submissions = 50 bogus top-100 entries/sec.
bottlenecks.symptom: Leaderboard top-100 fills with impossible scores overnight; community reports on forums; legitimate players drop off the visible board; support tickets spike.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Server-side sanity bounds per game_mode (reject score > mode_max), server-authoritative match validation (replay match_id against a match-server record of the session), key rotation per match with short TTLs, and SafetyNet/DeviceCheck attestation gating session key issuance.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on score submissions exceeding the 99.99th percentile of historical mode scores, or on (user_id, match_id) arriving without a matching match-server record within 60s. Track ZADD GT CH=1 rate for rank<100 — sudden spikes indicate top-board injection.

bottlenecks.title: Stale local cache shown after rank change
bottlenecks.trigger: Client renders last-known leaderboard immediately from local cache while refreshing in background. With 1s server-side cache TTL + ~100ms RTT + client render, user can see a 1–3s stale view. During tournaments (100K active viewers) the mismatch is visible when a WS rank_change event arrives before the background GET completes.
bottlenecks.symptom: User sees WS ticker announce 'rank 4321' but the rendered list still shows them at 9182 for 1–2s; players complain the leaderboard 'jumps' or 'lies'.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Reconcile strategy: when a WS rank_change event arrives, patch the in-memory list entry directly instead of waiting for the background GET; use the GET only as eventual truth. Also include generated_at in every response and discard responses older than the last applied WS event.
bottlenecks.detection: Client telemetry: log (ws_event_ts - next_get_apply_ts) distribution. Alert if p95 > 1500ms. Server-side, log Cache-Control hits vs WS event rate per user — high WS/GET ratio means clients are under-refreshing.

bottlenecks.title: WebSocket connection churn on mobile networks
bottlenecks.trigger: Mobile clients on cellular networks have NAT timeouts of 30–300s and frequent network transitions (wifi↔LTE). At 1M concurrent, even 1% reconnect/min = 10K reconnects/sec hitting the 20 WS nodes (~500/node/sec), each requiring a resubscribe and a full top-100 replay.
bottlenecks.symptom: During tournaments, users see the real-time ticker freeze for 5–30s, then a burst of events. WS fleet CPU spikes on reconnect storms; ingress LB shows 1K+ WS upgrades/sec.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Client-side: 30s heartbeat ping aligned with the server's, exponential backoff with jitter on reconnect (base 500ms, cap 10s), and resume tokens so the server can replay only events since last_seq rather than full state. Fall back to short-poll /v1/leaderboard/global every 2s when WS is unhealthy.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: ws_reconnects_per_user_per_hour — alert if p95 > 5/hr. Track upgrade_rate on the LB and subscribers_gauge on the WS fleet; a >20% dip correlated with a reconnect spike indicates a churn cascade.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Game Client is called out here In most system designs the client is "just the thing that calls the API," but for a **real-time gaming leaderboard** the client carries actual responsibility. Two things in particular: it **signs every score submission** (HMAC of match_id + score with a session key) because unsigned scores would let any player with a packet sniffer POST `score=999999999` and permanently poison the top-100, and it **chooses when to use WebSockets vs plain GETs** — during a tournament the client subscribes to live rank-change events, but on the lobby screen a one-shot GET is cheaper for everyone. The client is also where the "show last-known board instantly, refresh in background" trick lives, which is what makes a leaderboard *feel* real-time even when the server is 100ms away. ## What happens without a smart client If the client naively polled `/v1/leaderboard/global` every second on every screen, and trusted the server round-trip before rendering anything, users would see a blank leaderboard for ~150ms on every tab switch, and the read fleet would eat a flat 1 QPS *per user* instead of ~3 per session. ## The number that matters 10M daily players × 3 leaderboard views/session ÷ 86400s ≈ **350 QPS average, 500K QPS peak**. If the client didn't cache locally and instead polled once per second while the leaderboard screen was open, with 1M concurrent players that becomes **1,000,000 QPS sustained** — a 2× blow-up that would force the read tier and Redis cache to roughly double in size. ## Trade-off Pushing signing and caching into the client means trusting code running on a hostile device — hence the need for server-side score sanity bounds and match-server validation as a second line of defense.

lb.name: Load Balancer
lb.summary: L7 HTTPS load balancer distributing ingest and read traffic to separate API fleets.

sections.heading: Algorithm
sections.body: Round-robin per path prefix: `/v1/scores` routes to the ingest fleet, `/v1/leaderboard/*` routes to the read fleet. Keeps cache hit ratios on the read tier clean — ingest replicas have no reason to pull a leaderboard read.

sections.heading: WebSocket terminations
sections.body: Long-lived WS connections pin to the WebSocket fleet (separate backend pool) via consistent-hash on user_id. Upgrade requests bypass the short-request LB path.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body: Anycast VIP, multi-AZ HA pair. A dead ingest replica is ejected after 3 consecutive 5xx — worst case the client retries once.

bottlenecks.title: TLS termination CPU saturation at peak read+ingest
bottlenecks.trigger: Peak load is ~500K leaderboard reads/sec + ~50K score writes/sec = ~550K new HTTPS requests/sec hitting the LB. A typical L7 LB does ~20–40K TLS handshakes/sec per core; a short-lived client (cold session or post-DNS-TTL) storm during tournament start can push handshake rate to 50–100K/sec, saturating CPU.
bottlenecks.symptom: p99 TLS handshake latency jumps from ~5ms to >200ms; clients see SSL timeouts on tab open; LB CPU pegged at 100% on one AZ while the peer AZ is healthy; 5xx rate climbs even though backend replicas are idle.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable TLS session resumption (session tickets, 24h lifetime) and HTTP/2 multiplexing so one connection carries many reads; prefer ECDSA P-256 certs over RSA-2048 (3–5x cheaper handshakes); pre-warm the LB pool to 2x steady-state before scheduled tournament start; offload to dedicated TLS-accel instances (e.g. AWS NLB+ALB chain or Envoy with BoringSSL) if single-box CPU tops 70%.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on LB CPU > 70% for 1 min, ssl_handshakes_per_sec / requests_per_sec ratio > 0.3 (indicates poor resumption), and p99 ssl_handshake_time_ms > 50ms. Track new_connections_per_sec vs requests_per_sec on each LB node.

bottlenecks.title: WebSocket connection concentration on consistent-hash pool
bottlenecks.trigger: 1M concurrent WS connections pinned via consistent-hash(user_id) to 20 WS nodes = 50K conns/node. The LB holds these as long-lived upgraded sockets; each LB instance also keeps per-connection FD + buffer state. At ~1% reconnect/min (10K/sec during mobile network churn) the LB sees upgrade storms plus ephemeral-port/FD pressure.
bottlenecks.symptom: LB rejects new HTTP upgrades with 503 or TCP resets; healthy short-request API traffic begins to see connect failures because the LB has exhausted ephemeral ports toward upstream WS nodes; tournament viewers report the live ticker goes silent and won't reconnect.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Separate the WS-terminating LB tier from the short-request LB tier (different VIPs, different fleets) so WS FD exhaustion can't starve /v1/scores and /v1/leaderboard/*. Raise per-node FD limit to 1M, set SO_REUSEPORT, and pre-provision ephemeral port range 1024–65535 toward upstream. Route upgrades via a dedicated NLB (L4) to skip L7 parsing cost on the long-lived path.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on lb_established_connections > 80% of configured max_connections per node, ephemeral_port_usage > 70%, and ws_upgrade_rate > 2K/sec sustained. Track tcp_resets_sent and 503 rate specifically on the /ws upgrade path.

bottlenecks.title: Cross-AZ failover cold pool after single LB failure
bottlenecks.trigger: Design uses a multi-AZ HA pair with anycast VIP. When the active LB fails, all 550K req/sec + 1M WS conns shift to the peer within ~3s. The peer's connection table, TLS session cache, and backend health-check state are cold, so the first minute sees 2x handshake cost and full backend reconnects from every client.
bottlenecks.symptom: During failover, observed p99 latency spike from ~10ms to 500ms+ for 30–60s; backends see a synchronous surge of new TCP/TLS connections; read API reports a brief 5xx spike even though Redis and DB are unaffected; WS subscribers all reconnect simultaneously, triggering the resubscribe-storm mitigation in the WS tier.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run active-active both AZs behind anycast (not active-passive) so each node is warm at 50% utilization — failover doubles load but doesn't cold-start anything. Share TLS session tickets via a common key (rotated hourly) between LB nodes so clients resume on the peer without a full handshake. Ensure backend health checks run from both LBs continuously, not just the active one.
bottlenecks.detection: Synthetic probe every 10s measuring handshake + first-byte latency through both VIPs; alert if either shows >5x its 1h baseline. Track cross-AZ connection_migration_rate during failover drills; aim for failover p99 spike < 100ms.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Load Balancer is here For a real-time leaderboard serving 1M concurrent players, no single API server can handle the traffic — and more importantly, the **write traffic (score submissions) looks completely different from the read traffic (leaderboard views)**. Score submissions are bursty and CPU-heavy (HMAC verification, Redis ZADD, DB buffering); leaderboard reads are tiny and cache-friendly. The LB here doesn't just spread load — it **routes `/v1/scores` to the ingest fleet and `/v1/leaderboard/*` to the read fleet**, keeping those two worlds isolated. WebSocket upgrades get pinned via consistent-hash on `user_id` to a third fleet so long-lived connections don't mingle with short requests. ## What happens without it Without the LB, you'd either point DNS at one API box (which dies instantly at tournament start) or run both workloads on the same shared fleet. In the shared case, a tournament spike of 50K score submissions/sec would burn CPU on HMAC verification and starve the read path — players tapping the leaderboard tab would see 2–5 second hangs or outright timeouts, while operators would see ingest replicas healthy but reads queuing. One noisy workload would drag down the other. ## The number Peak load is ~500K reads/sec + ~50K writes/sec = **~550K requests/sec** hitting the front door. Split across the two backend pools, the read fleet handles ~500K/sec at ~3ms each (needing ~1,500 concurrent slots), and ingest handles ~50K/sec at ~3ms each (~150 slots). Routing by path means each fleet sizes independently: you don't over-provision ingest just because reads spiked. ## Trade-off The LB itself becomes the new single point of failure, which is why the design runs an active-active multi-AZ pair with anycast.

ingest.name: Score Ingest API
ingest.summary: Stateless service validating and persisting score submissions; writes to Redis ZSET + durable DB.

sections.heading: Endpoint
sections.body:
```
POST /v1/scores
{ "user_id": "u_18232", "game_mode": "ranked_duel", "score": 42815, "match_id": "m_8f12a9", "region": "us-west", "client_sig": "hmac_sha256:..."
}
```

sections.heading: Write path
sections.body:
1. Verify HMAC against the session's server-side signing key (anti-cheat)
2. Deduplicate on (user_id, match_id) — idempotent replay
3. ZADD GT on the appropriate leaderboard key (only write if the new score is higher)
4. INSERT into durable scores DB (async, fire-and-forget with local durable buffer)
5. Emit WS event if the ZADD actually changed a rank inside top-K

sections.heading: ZADD GT
sections.body: `ZADD <key> GT <score> <member>` only updates if the new score beats the existing one. Avoids the read-modify-write race that plain ZADD would have under concurrent submissions for the same user.

sections.heading: Horizontal scaling
sections.body: Stateless → scale on CPU. Peak 50K write QPS * ~3ms service time → ~150 concurrent req/replica → ~20 replicas at safe utilization.

gained: Survives Redis outage without rejecting writes
Decouples spiky client load from Redis shape
lost: Requires a consumer to apply ZADDs

bottlenecks.title: Synchronous HMAC verification saturates CPU at tournament peak
bottlenecks.trigger: Peak 50K score submissions/sec each require an HMAC-SHA256 verify + dedup Bloom check + 3 parallel ZADD GT calls (global, region, mode) + WAL append. At ~3ms service time and ~150 concurrent slots/replica, the sized ~20 replicas run at ~75% CPU headroom; a 1.5x tournament overshoot (75K/sec) pushes CPU past 90% and service time balloons from 3ms to 20ms+.
bottlenecks.symptom: p99 POST /v1/scores latency jumps from ~15ms to 200ms+; ingest replicas show CPU pegged at 100%; LB begins ejecting replicas on 5xx, shifting load to survivors in a cascading brownout; clients see submission timeouts and retry, amplifying load another 20–30%.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Pre-scale to 30 replicas (not 20) before known tournament windows based on event schedule; switch HMAC to BLAKE3 or a hardware-accelerated AES-GMAC (2–4x faster than SHA-256); add HPA on CPU > 60% with 60s scale-up; shed load at the LB by returning 429 with Retry-After when ingest CPU > 85% rather than letting latency collapse.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on ingest_cpu_avg > 70% for 2 min, p99 POST /v1/scores > 50ms, and http_5xx_rate > 0.5%. Track hmac_verify_duration_p99 separately — if it exceeds 2ms, CPU is the bottleneck not Redis.

bottlenecks.title: Local WAL data loss on ingest replica crash
bottlenecks.trigger: Ingest buffers DB writes in a local WAL, flushing to the scores DB in 50-row batches every ~50ms. At 50K writes/sec across 20 replicas, each replica holds ~125 rows in-flight at any moment; an OOM kill, kubelet eviction, or AZ failure wipes the WAL before flush. During tournaments (peak 50K/sec), a single replica loss drops ~125 scores; a full AZ outage mid-tournament can drop 2500+ scores including potentially top-100 entries.
bottlenecks.symptom: Player reports 'I got a 95000 but the leaderboard still shows my old 42000' — Redis ZADD succeeded but the durable record is gone, so the nightly snapshot rebuild silently regresses the user's score. Support tickets spike 24h after any replica restart; audit logs show Redis/DB divergence at the (user_id, match_id) grain.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Replace in-memory WAL with fsync'd local disk WAL (tmpfs → persistent volume) with fsync every 10 rows OR 10ms — adds ~1ms latency but survives crash. Alternatively adopt the `ingest-queue` alternative (Kafka) as the durable buffer so ingest replicas are truly stateless. Make pod shutdown hooks drain WAL to DB with 30s graceful termination.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: wal_pending_rows_gauge per replica — alert if > 500 (indicates flush is lagging). Daily reconciliation job that compares Redis ZSET scores vs best_scores table and alerts on any (user_id) where Redis > DB (signals lost DB write). Track pod_termination_wal_flush_complete_ratio — must be >99.9%.

bottlenecks.title: Dedup Bloom filter false positives force DB exists-checks at peak
bottlenecks.trigger: Per-replica Bloom filter of recent (user_id, match_id) submissions sized for ~1M entries at 1% FPR. At 50K submissions/sec, 1% = 500 false positives/sec/replica × 20 replicas = 10K unnecessary `db.exists_score` lookups/sec hitting the scores DB. These are on the synchronous ingest hot path (blocking client response) and compete with the 50K async INSERT batches for DB connections.
bottlenecks.symptom: During peak tournament traffic, DB connection pool saturates on the primary; ingest p99 latency grows from 15ms to 80ms with DB query_wait_ms dominating the trace; INSERT batch flush falls behind and wal_pending grows, compounding risk of bottleneck #2.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Lower Bloom FPR to 0.01% (10x more memory, ~10 MB/replica — trivial) so false positives drop to 5/sec/replica. Add a second-tier LRU cache of 'confirmed NOT duplicate' (user_id, match_id) hashes to absorb the residual misses. Route exists-checks to a read replica instead of the primary. Use `INSERT... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` alone and rely on the unique constraint for idempotency, skipping the pre-check entirely when the Bloom says 'might'.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: dedup_db_lookup_rate — alert if > 100/sec/replica (indicates FPR drift or hot user). Track (dedup_db_lookups / submissions) ratio; baseline should be < 0.0001. Alert on db_primary_connection_pool_utilization > 80% during non-batch intervals.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a dedicated Score Ingest API For a real-time leaderboard, every match that ends produces a score that needs to land in the ranking structure *fast* — and you cannot trust the client to tell the truth. The Ingest API is the chokepoint that does four things no other component can: it **verifies the HMAC signature** (so a hacked client can't POST `score=999999999`), **deduplicates on `(user_id, match_id)`** so a retried submission doesn't double-count, **writes to Redis with `ZADD GT`** so only genuine improvements update the board, and **decides whether a WebSocket push is worth firing**. Mixing this logic into the read path or doing it in the client would either leak trust or slow every leaderboard view. ## What happens without it If clients wrote directly to Redis, within a day the top-100 would be filled with `INT_MAX` scores from anyone who sniffed the protocol, and the same match retried three times would show up three times in the history table. Operators would see Redis and the DB disagree constantly, and legitimate players would abandon the game. If instead you folded ingest into the read API, a tournament write storm would starve leaderboard reads — tapping the Leaderboard tab would hang for seconds. ## The number Peak write load is **~50K score submissions/sec** during tournaments. At ~3ms service time per request (HMAC verify + ZADD + WAL append), each replica handles ~150 concurrent in-flight requests, so 50,000 × 0.003 / 150 ≈ **~20 replicas** keep up with safe headroom. Because the service is stateless, you scale it on CPU alone. ## Trade-off Splitting ingest from reads doubles the fleet count and the deploy surface, but it's the only way to keep a write spike from taking down the read path.

read.name: Leaderboard Read API
read.summary: Stateless service returning top-K, region boards, and a player's rank + neighbors.

sections.heading: Endpoints
sections.body:
```
GET /v1/leaderboard/global?top=100
GET /v1/leaderboard/region/{region}?top=100
GET /v1/leaderboard/user/{user_id}?window=5 # user's rank + 5 above + 5 below
```

sections.heading: Top-K path
sections.body:
1. Check Redis cache for top-100 JSON blob (key `lb:global:top100`, TTL 1s)
2. On miss: `ZREVRANGE leaderboard:global 0 99 WITHSCORES` + hydrate user display names
3. Cache result with 1s TTL — absorbs the hot read storm behind a single Redis hop

sections.heading: User-rank path
sections.body:
```
rank = ZREVRANK leaderboard:global u_18232 # e.g. 4321
if rank is None: user unranked
start = max(0, rank - 5)
stop = rank + 5
ZREVRANGE leaderboard:global start stop WITHSCORES # 11 entries centered on user
```

sections.heading: Latency budget
sections.body: Top-K cache hit: ~2ms. Top-K cache miss: ~5–8ms (one Redis ZRANGE + display-name hydrate). User-rank: ~3–6ms (two Redis ops, both O(log N)).

bottlenecks.title: Cache-miss stampede on TTL rollover at 500K QPS
bottlenecks.trigger: The lb:global:top100 blob has a 1s TTL. At peak 500K reads/sec, roughly 500 concurrent requests arrive within the ~1ms window between expiry and re-fill. Without strict single-flight coalescing, every replica (~50+ read replicas sized for 500K QPS at ~3ms each) races to issue ZREVRANGE 0 99 + 100-key MGET against Redis — a 50x amplification on the ZSET node exactly when it's already hot.
bottlenecks.symptom: Every second, Redis ZSET CPU spikes to 100% for ~10ms; read API p99 latency oscillates between 5ms (hit) and 80–200ms (miss storm); X-Cache:MISS rate exceeds 0.5% (should be <0.01%); users see the leaderboard tab stall once per second during tournaments.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Implement process-local single-flight (e.g. Go singleflight, Java CompletableFuture dedup) keyed on lb:global:top100 so only one goroutine per replica fetches on miss. Layer a distributed lock via SET NX PX 200 lb:global:top100:lock so only one replica across the fleet rebuilds. Use early-expiration refresh (rebuild at 80% TTL in the background) so the cache is never actually empty. Add 100–200ms jitter to per-replica TTLs.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on cache_miss_rate > 0.1% on lb:global:top100, redis_zset_cpu p99 > 60%, and p99_latency_ratio(miss:hit) > 20x. Track zrevrange_global_top100_rate — should be ~1/sec across the entire fleet, not ~50/sec.

bottlenecks.title: Display-name MGET amplification on user-rank path
bottlenecks.trigger: Every /v1/leaderboard/user/{id}?window=5 issues a pipelined MGET of 11 display-name keys against the read-side Redis cache. At steady state user-rank reads are ~10–20% of the 500K peak = 50–100K QPS, producing 550K–1.1M MGET subkey lookups/sec. A 5-minute TTL plus name-change or cold-user traffic (e.g. post-season reset) drops hit rate from ~99% to ~80%, forcing fallback DB lookups for display names on the hot read path.
bottlenecks.symptom: p99 /v1/leaderboard/user/* latency climbs from ~6ms to 30–60ms; Redis cache CPU shows MGET dominating; scores DB sees unexpected SELECT bursts on user profile tables; on-call sees correlated latency spikes after every season rollover or bulk display-name update.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Batch-warm user:*:display into Redis from the best_scores working set after snapshot rebuilds. Increase TTL to 1 hour with explicit invalidation on profile update events. Embed display_name directly in the ZSET member encoding (e.g. member = 'u_18232|AceAlpha42') to eliminate the second hop entirely — trades ~30 bytes/entry extra memory (~3GB at 100M) for zero hydration latency. Add a local in-process LRU (10K entries) per read replica for ultra-hot names.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: display_name_cache_hit_rate — alert if < 98%. Track mget_duration_p99 per request and the ratio (display_fetch_ms / total_request_ms) — alert if > 40%. Log db_fallback_name_lookups_per_sec — should be near zero.

bottlenecks.title: Coupled failure with Redis ZSET/Cache during failover
bottlenecks.trigger: The read API has no independent data path — every cache miss requires Redis ZSET, every hit still requires Redis cache. During Sentinel-driven failover (~3s per shard) or an AZ partition, both the cache and the ZSET replica on that AZ become unavailable. At 500K QPS, 3s of unavailability = ~1.5M in-flight requests with no fallback, while the surviving replica suddenly absorbs 2x load cold.
bottlenecks.symptom: During Redis failover drills, read API returns 503/504 for 3–10s; the load balancer ejects read replicas that time out waiting on Redis; clients see the 'last-known leaderboard' frozen for ~10s; post-failover Redis CPU stays at 90%+ for 30s as caches repopulate.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a last-resort in-process LRU on each read replica caching lb:global:top100 for up to 5s with a stale-while-failover flag — serve stale with X-Stale:true header rather than 503. Configure Redis client with fast-fail timeouts (50ms) and automatic fallback to the replica read endpoint. Pre-warm replica caches via continuous shadow reads. Run the cache tier active-active across AZs rather than primary-replica.
bottlenecks.detection: Synthetic probe of /v1/leaderboard/global every 1s with alert on any response > 200ms or non-200. Track redis_client_timeout_rate and stale_response_served_rate. Drill: force monthly Redis failover and measure read p99 — target < 500ms during the 3s window.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a dedicated Read API for this leaderboard For a real-time leaderboard serving 10M daily players, the read patterns are **wildly different from the write patterns**, and they're also different from each other. "Give me the top-100 globally" is a request the entire world is asking for the same answer to — it should be cached aggressively and served as a pre-rendered blob. "Give me user u_18232's rank and neighbors" is unique per user and can't be cached the same way. The Read API is where this branching logic lives: it decides when to hand back a cached JSON blob versus when to run `ZREVRANK` + `ZREVRANGE` against Redis and hydrate display names. It's also a stateless shock absorber — you can scale it on CPU without touching Redis or the DB. ## What happens without it If clients talked to Redis directly, every tab-open at tournament start would issue a `ZREVRANGE 0 99` against the ZSET — and at peak, that's 500K identical queries per second hammering one Redis node that was happily doing writes at 50K/sec. Redis CPU pegs, ingest latency spikes because `ZADD` is queued behind reads, and the leaderboard freezes for everyone. Operators would see Redis saturated while the actual *useful* work (unique queries) is drowned out by duplicates. ## The number Peak read load is **~500K requests/sec**, but the top-100 board only *changes* a few times per second. A 1-second cache TTL on `lb:global:top100` means Redis sees ~1 `ZREVRANGE`/sec instead of 500,000 — a **500,000× reduction** in ZSET load, turning an impossible query pattern into a trivial one. ## Trade-off That 1-second TTL means a player can see a leaderboard up to ~1 second stale — acceptable here, and the WebSocket push handles the cases where it isn't.

zset.name: Redis Sorted Set (ZSET)
zset.summary: In-memory skiplist-backed sorted set holding (user_id, score) — the hot, authoritative ranking structure.

sections.heading: Data layout
sections.body:
One ZSET per scope:
- `leaderboard:global` — all users
- `leaderboard:region:us-west` — per region
- `leaderboard:mode:ranked_duel` — per game mode
Each entry: member = user_id (string, ~8 bytes), score = float64. Overhead ~80 bytes per entry including skiplist nodes → 8 GB for 100M users.

sections.heading: Complexity
sections.body:
```
ZADD O(log N) insert or update score
ZREVRANGE O(log N + M) top-M by score desc
ZREVRANK O(log N) rank of a member
ZINCRBY O(log N) atomic delta update
```
At N=100M, log N ≈ 27 — every op is sub-ms on commodity hardware.

sections.heading: Persistence + HA
sections.body: AOF appendfsync=everysec (≤1s data loss on crash) + Redis replication (1 replica per shard for reads; primary fails over in ~3s via Sentinel). Not a durable store — SQL DB is the system of record.

sections.heading: Sharding
sections.body: Leaderboards are naturally sharded by scope (region, mode), so no cross-shard ZRANGE needed. If the global board grows past one node, use a top-N-of-N-shards scatter-gather — but at 100M members 8 GB still fits one node comfortably.

gained: Single source of truth; no Redis to run
lost: O(N log N) per read — dies at 100M rows
Cannot cheaply compute user rank without a full scan or pre-computed rank column

gained: Rich filter + sort on many fields
Handles very large boards without full recompute
lost: 10x Redis op cost for hot top-K

bottlenecks.title: Single-node ZSET CPU saturation from hot global board
bottlenecks.trigger: The global ZSET lives on one primary (8 GB fits one node). At peak it absorbs 50K ZADD GT/sec from ingest (3 parallel ZADDs per submission → 150K ops/sec including region+mode shards on the same node) plus ~1 coalesced ZREVRANGE/sec from the read cache refresh, plus ZREVRANK + ZREVRANGE for every user-rank request (~50–100K/sec at peak). Redis is single-threaded per shard; a mixed op profile at ~200K ops/sec per primary pushes the event loop past 80% CPU.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis INFO shows used_cpu_sys climbing past 80%; slowlog fills with ZREVRANGE entries >5ms; ingest p99 latency jumps from 3ms to 50ms+ as ZADDs queue behind reads; read API cache-miss rebuilds take 20–50ms instead of 1.5ms; tournament score submissions visibly lag on the leaderboard.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Split the single logical `leaderboard:global` across N shards using scatter-gather top-K-of-N (e.g. 4 shards by hash(user_id)%4, each returning top-100, then merge on the read API). Pin region and mode ZSETs to separate Redis nodes so their ops don't contend with global. Enable Redis 7 IO threads for network offload. Use ZADD with multiple score/member pairs batched per pipeline to amortize command parsing.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on redis_cpu_usage > 70% sustained 1 min, redis_commands_per_sec > 150K per shard, and slowlog_len growth rate > 10/min with ZREVRANGE/ZREVRANK as top offenders. Track instantaneous_ops_per_sec vs p99 command latency — any correlation above ~120K ops/sec indicates the single-thread ceiling is near.

bottlenecks.title: AOF everysec data loss + failover gap during tournaments
bottlenecks.trigger: Persistence is AOF appendfsync=everysec with Sentinel failover in ~3s. At peak 50K ZADD/sec, a primary crash loses up to 1s × 50K = 50,000 score updates from the AOF buffer, and the 3s failover window drops another ~150K ZADDs silently (ingest writes to the dead primary fail; WAL retries eventually reach the DB but Redis ZSET is now behind). Top-100 tournament entries submitted in that window simply disappear from the board until the nightly rebuild.
bottlenecks.symptom: Post-failover, users report 'my winning score vanished' or top-100 shows yesterday's leaders; Redis ZSET scores for recent (user_id) are lower than best_scores table; ingest error rate spikes for 3s during failover; support tickets cluster around the failover timestamp.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run an emergency ZSET rebuild triggered by Sentinel +switch-master event rather than waiting for the nightly job — replay best_scores WHERE updated_at > (failover_time - 10min) in ~30s. Move to appendfsync=always for the global board during scheduled tournaments (accepts 2x write latency for zero loss). Deploy Redis in active-active via CRDTs (Redis Enterprise) or dual-write from ingest to two independent primaries and take MAX on read.
bottlenecks.detection: Continuous reconciliation job comparing ZSCORE leaderboard:global vs best_scores.best_score for a sampled 10K users every 60s — alert on any user where ZSCORE < DB score (indicates lost ZADD). Track sentinel_failover_count and correlate with zset_db_divergence_count spikes.

bottlenecks.title: Memory growth past single-node limit as user base expands
bottlenecks.trigger: Current sizing: 100M members × ~80 bytes = 8 GB, comfortable on one node. But the design declares 10 regional boards + per-mode boards + per-friend-group boards — if each of 10 regions holds ~10M members and 5 game modes hold 100M each, total ZSET memory across all scopes is 8 GB (global) + 10 × 0.8 GB (regions) + 5 × 8 GB (modes) = ~56 GB. At 20% YoY growth or a new game mode launch, a single 64 GB Redis node crosses the 75% maxmemory threshold where fork for BGSAVE doubles RSS and OOM-kills the process.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis used_memory_rss approaches maxmemory; BGSAVE fails with 'Cannot allocate memory'; AOF rewrite stalls; during traffic spikes Redis starts evicting or returns OOM errors to ZADD; latency jumps because the kernel swaps or the process is restarted by the OOM killer.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard each large ZSET (global, per-mode) across 4–8 Redis Cluster nodes via scatter-gather; a top-100 query fans out to all shards, each returns its local top-100, merge in the read API in O(N_shards × 100). Use Redis Cluster with hash-tagged keys `{mode:ranked_duel}:shard:0..7`. Tune `maxmemory` to 60% of RAM to leave headroom for fork. Periodically TRIM inactive users (not played in 90 days) from non-global boards using ZREMRANGEBYRANK.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on redis_used_memory_rss / maxmemory > 0.70, rdb_last_bgsave_status!= ok, and mem_fragmentation_ratio > 1.5. Track zset_cardinality per key weekly — alert if any ZSET exceeds 50M entries, which is the scatter-gather trigger point.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a Redis ZSET for this leaderboard The hard part of a real-time leaderboard isn't *storing* scores — any database can do that. The hard part is answering **"what rank is user u_18232 out of 100 million?"** in under 10 milliseconds, while 50,000 new scores per second are being written. A ZSET is a skiplist keyed by score, so it keeps every player pre-sorted at all times. Inserting a new score, finding someone's rank, and grabbing the top-100 are all O(log N) — roughly 27 hops at 100M users. That's the whole reason this component exists: it turns ranking from an expensive query into a cheap pointer walk. ## What happens without it If you served ranks straight from the SQL scores table, every "where am I?" tap would run `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM scores WHERE score >?` across 100M rows, or worse, an `ORDER BY score LIMIT 100`. Users would see the leaderboard tab spin for 2–10 seconds, operators would watch the DB primary pin at 100% CPU, and the ingest path would slow to a crawl because writes are competing with giant read scans. One tournament would take the whole game offline. ## The number Peak read load is **~500K leaderboard requests/sec**. A ZREVRANGE for top-100 costs O(log N + 100) ≈ ~130 operations on the skiplist, running sub-millisecond. The equivalent SQL sort over 100M rows is ~2.7 billion comparisons per query — physically impossible at that QPS. ## The trade-off Redis is in-memory and not durable on its own, so the SQL DB stays as system-of-record and a snapshot job rebuilds the ZSET if Redis ever loses data.

db.name: Scores DB (durable)
db.summary: Source-of-truth SQL store holding every score submission for durability, audit, and snapshot rebuild.

sections.heading: Schema
sections.body:
```
TABLE scores id BIGSERIAL PK user_id BIGINT match_id UUID game_mode TEXT region TEXT score INT submitted_at TIMESTAMP UNIQUE (user_id, match_id) -- idempotency INDEX (user_id, submitted_at DESC) -- history queries TABLE best_scores user_id BIGINT game_mode TEXT region TEXT best_score INT updated_at TIMESTAMP PRIMARY KEY (user_id, game_mode)
```
`best_scores` is a materialized view that the snapshot job uses to rebuild the Redis ZSET.

sections.heading: Why SQL
sections.body:
- Unique constraint on (user_id, match_id) kills duplicate submissions at the DB layer
- Range scans for user history / season archives
- Sharded by user_id hash once a single primary saturates (~200K write QPS)

sections.heading: Write path
sections.body: Ingest API writes asynchronously — scores are first buffered in a local WAL on the ingest replica, then flushed to the DB in 50-row batches. Rides through 30s DB hiccups without dropping writes.

sections.heading: Consistency
sections.body: DB and Redis can diverge briefly (Redis write succeeds, DB flush is in-flight). The snapshot job converges them hourly. A crash during the window loses <30s of scores — acceptable for a game leaderboard.

lost: Secondary-index scans on region leaderboards are costly

bottlenecks.title: Write primary saturation at tournament peak
bottlenecks.trigger: Peak ingest is 50K score submissions/sec, each producing one INSERT into scores and one UPSERT into best_scores = ~100K write ops/sec sustained. A single PostgreSQL/MySQL primary tops out around 50–80K write TPS with WAL fsync; batching at 50 rows/50ms from 20 ingest replicas still means ~2K batch commits/sec plus 50K best_scores UPSERTs fighting for the same row locks on hot users.
bottlenecks.symptom: DB primary CPU pegs at 95%+, WAL disk latency p99 climbs from 2ms to 50ms, ingest WAL backlog grows (wal_pending_rows metric rising), best_scores UPSERT lock waits appear in pg_stat_activity, and score-to-leaderboard divergence widens because the snapshot job can't keep pace.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard scores and best_scores by hash(user_id) across 4–8 primaries (design already calls this out at ~200K QPS — pre-shard before tournaments rather than reactively). Drop best_scores UPSERT from the synchronous path and compute it in a CDC consumer (Debezium → Kafka → best_scores writer). Use unlogged staging tables for scores and move to logged via periodic MERGE. Enable group commit / synchronous_commit=off for scores (acceptable given the <30s loss tolerance).
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on db_write_tps > 60K/sec sustained 1 min, wal_fsync_p99 > 20ms, pg_stat_activity rows waiting on best_scores_pkey lock > 50, and ingest wal_pending_rows_gauge > 1000 per replica.

bottlenecks.title: UNIQUE (user_id, match_id) index bloat and hot-leaf contention
bottlenecks.trigger: At 50K inserts/sec × 86400s = 4.3B rows/day peak, the UNIQUE (user_id, match_id) btree grows ~200 GB/month and every INSERT traverses + locks a leaf page. With match_id as a UUID, inserts scatter randomly across the index causing full random-IO writes; at 50K/sec this exceeds typical NVMe random-write IOPS budgets (~100K) once the index exceeds RAM (~128 GB buffer pool).
bottlenecks.symptom: INSERT latency p99 climbs from 5ms to 100ms+ after index exceeds memory, buffer cache hit ratio drops below 95%, autovacuum falls behind and index bloat grows to 2–3x logical size, ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING checks become the dominant cost in pg_stat_statements.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Switch match_id ordering to a time-prefixed ULID/Snowflake so inserts hit the index tail (sequential writes instead of random). Partition scores by submitted_at (monthly ranges) so hot partition fits in RAM while old partitions stay cold and detachable for archival. Move dedup check out of the DB entirely — rely on the ingest Bloom + ZADD GT idempotency and let scores be append-only without the UNIQUE constraint, enforcing idempotency via a short-TTL dedup Redis set instead.
bottlenecks.detection: Track pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_blks_read rate (should be near zero if index is in cache), alert on buffer_cache_hit_ratio < 98%, monitor index_bloat_pct > 30%, and watch INSERT p99 latency per ingest batch.

bottlenecks.title: Storage and retention growth outpacing single-cluster capacity
bottlenecks.trigger: Design estimates 3.6 TB/year of scores at current daily load, but peak 50K/sec × 200 bytes = 10 MB/sec = ~315 TB/year raw during sustained tournament seasons — nearly 100x the baseline estimate. The scores table plus its index plus best_scores plus WAL retention can exceed 1 TB within weeks of a viral growth spike, pushing a single primary past reasonable vacuum/backup windows.
bottlenecks.symptom: pg_dump backup duration exceeds 24h, PITR WAL retention consumes >50% of disk, autovacuum on scores never completes a full pass (last_autovacuum stale > 7 days), snapshot rebuild job scan of best_scores takes >30 min instead of the planned 10, and season-rollover TRUNCATE/archive jobs block live writes.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Implement declarative partitioning by (game_mode, month) with automatic detach-and-archive to S3/Parquet after 90 days — keep only hot partitions in the primary. Move historical scores to a columnar store (ClickHouse/BigQuery) via CDC for audit/history queries, leaving the OLTP DB with ~30 days of data (~25–260 GB depending on traffic). Use logical replication slots with bounded retention to prevent WAL from filling disk during consumer lag.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on db_disk_used_pct > 70%, pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup on scores > 100M, replication_slot_lag_bytes > 50 GB, and hot-partition size growth rate > 10 GB/day (triggers early partition rotation).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Scores DB is here The real-time leaderboard lives in Redis — that's what makes ranking fast. But Redis is an **in-memory** store: if the node crashes, restarts, or gets evicted, every score vanishes. For a game where players grind for weeks to climb a ranked ladder, losing their progress is unacceptable. The Scores DB is the **system of record** that Redis is *not*: every submission lands here durably, with a `UNIQUE (user_id, match_id)` constraint that makes retries idempotent, and a `best_scores` table that the snapshot job uses to rebuild the ZSET from scratch if Redis ever loses data. It also holds the history you need for season archives, audit (e.g. "is this score legit?"), and cheating investigations — things the ZSET deliberately doesn't store. ## What happens without it Picture a Redis primary OOM-killing itself mid-tournament. Without the durable DB, the top-100 is gone — not stale, *gone*. Players reopen the app and see an empty board or yesterday's cached snapshot. Support gets flooded ("where's my rank?"), and operators have no way to reconstruct state because the ingest path wrote only to memory. The snapshot job would have nothing to replay from. ## The number At peak, ingest handles **50K submissions/sec**, each ~200 bytes → ~10 MB/sec → roughly **3.6 TB/year** of history. The design batches these into 50-row inserts every ~50ms, which drops the DB's effective commit rate from 50K/sec to ~1,000 batched commits/sec — well within a single SQL primary's budget until you shard by `user_id` hash. ## Trade-off Async DB writes mean Redis and the DB can diverge by up to ~30 seconds during a crash — the designer traded perfect durability for ingest latency, which is fine for a game but would be wrong for a bank.

cache.name: Redis Cache (read-side)
cache.summary: Short-TTL cache of pre-rendered leaderboard responses, fronting the ZSET to absorb read storms.

sections.heading: What's cached
sections.body:
- `lb:global:top100` → JSON body of the top-100 response (TTL 1s)
- `lb:region:{region}:top100` → per-region top-100 (TTL 1s)
- `user:{user_id}:display` → display name + avatar URL (TTL 5 min)

sections.heading: Why 1-second TTL
sections.body: Freshness target is < 1s. A 1s TTL gives a worst-case perceived lag of 2s (just-missed write + full TTL), which is fine for a leaderboard that usually only changes on the top-K boundary during tournaments.

sections.heading: Stampede protection
sections.body: Request coalescing in the read API: when the cache key expires, one in-flight Redis ZRANGE serves all concurrent misses. Prevents a 500K-QPS thundering herd from crushing Redis on every TTL rollover.

bottlenecks.title: Thundering-herd stampede on 1s TTL rollover
bottlenecks.trigger: The lb:global:top100 key expires every 1s. At 500K reads/sec, ~500 requests arrive within a ~1ms window of expiry. If request coalescing is implemented per-replica only (not globally), 50+ read replicas each fire a ZREVRANGE + 100-key MGET simultaneously, causing a 50x op amplification on the ZSET every second.
bottlenecks.symptom: Periodic 1Hz latency sawtooth on /v1/leaderboard/global (p99 swings 5ms→80ms once per second); ZSET CPU shows 1Hz spike pattern; X-Cache:MISS rate >0.1% instead of near-zero; slowlog fills with ZREVRANGE entries aligned with TTL boundaries.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Implement two-tier stampede protection: (1) per-replica singleflight keyed on cache key so only one goroutine/thread per replica misses, (2) distributed lock via SET NX PX 200 lb:global:top100:lock so only one replica across the fleet rebuilds. Use early-expiration refresh at 80% TTL (rebuild at 800ms, serve cached until 1s) so the cache is never actually empty. Add ±100ms jitter to SETEX TTLs.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on cache_miss_rate{key='lb:global:top100'} > 0.1%, zrevrange_global_top100_rate > 2/sec fleetwide (baseline ~1/sec), and ratio p99_miss_latency/p99_hit_latency > 20x. Plot request rate vs time-mod-1s and alert on 1Hz periodicity in p99.

bottlenecks.title: Cache node bandwidth saturation serving 14KB top-100 blobs
bottlenecks.trigger: Top-100 response blob is ~14.8KB (per op walkthrough). At 500K reads/sec with near-100% cache hit rate, outbound traffic from the cache node is 500,000 × 14.8KB = 7.4 GB/sec = ~60 Gbps, far exceeding a single Redis node's typical 10–25 Gbps NIC budget. Even with the read API fleet absorbing most via its own local cache, residual traffic to Redis at 50K QPS = 740 MB/sec = ~6 Gbps starts to saturate.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis client_output_buffer grows; net_output_bytes metric pegged; p99 GET latency climbs from 1ms to 10–30ms with no CPU increase; tcp_retransmits spike on the Redis node's NIC; read API replicas see timeouts clustered on the cache GET, not the ZSET ops.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a process-local L1 cache (Caffeine/Ristretto) on every read API replica with 500ms TTL and ~200 entries — collapses 500K/sec fleetwide into ~2 cache GETs/sec/replica. Compress the blob with zstd (14.8KB → ~3KB for repetitive user_id/name data). Shard the cache tier by key-space hash across 3–4 nodes so bandwidth distributes. Return Cache-Control: max-age=1 so CDN/client-side caches absorb another layer.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on redis_net_output_bytes_per_sec > 5 Gbps per node, instantaneous_output_kbps sustained > 70% of NIC capacity, and client_output_buffer_length p99 > 1MB. Track (cache_gets_per_sec × avg_value_bytes) and alert before hitting 80% of NIC.

bottlenecks.title: user:{id}:display cold-cache storm after season rollover or deploy
bottlenecks.trigger: The user:{id}:display keys have 5-minute TTL and back the top-100 render + user-rank ±5 window hydration. After a cache flush (deploy, failover, season rollover at 100M users), the first ZREVRANGE rebuild MGETs 100 cold keys; concurrently ~50–100K user-rank reads/sec each MGET 11 cold keys = 550K–1.1M DB-fallback lookups/sec hitting the scores/profile DB before the cache warms.
bottlenecks.symptom: Immediately after deploy or Redis failover: user-rank p99 jumps from 6ms to 100–300ms for 2–5 min; scores DB CPU spikes with SELECT bursts on user profile lookups; cache_miss_rate{pattern='user:*:display'} jumps from <1% to 20–40%; support sees 'leaderboard loading forever' reports clustered at deploy time.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Pre-warm user:*:display for the top 100K active users as part of the deploy/failover playbook by replaying from best_scores + a bulk MSET pipeline (~30s). Increase display TTL to 1 hour with explicit invalidation via pub/sub on profile updates. Consider embedding display_name directly in ZSET members (member = 'u_18232|AceAlpha42') to eliminate the hydration hop entirely — costs ~3GB extra memory at 100M but zero cold-start risk.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: display_cache_hit_rate — alert if < 95% sustained 30s. Track db_profile_lookup_rate with alert > 1K/sec (should be near zero in steady state). Add a deploy hook that blocks cutover until pre-warm MSET pipeline reports >90% coverage of the top-100K active user set.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a separate read-side cache for this leaderboard For a real-time gaming leaderboard, the dirty secret of the top-100 global board is that **everybody is asking the same question**. When 10 million daily players tap the Leaderboard tab, they all want the identical list of 100 names. The ZSET itself is fast — a `ZREVRANGE 0 99` is ~1.5ms — but it still has to walk the skiplist, fetch 100 members, and the read API still has to hydrate 100 display names and serialize JSON every single time. Doing that 500,000 times per second per unique query is wasteful when the answer barely changes. The read-side cache stores the **already-rendered JSON response** so that 99.9% of reads are a single O(1) Redis GET and a byte copy out to the client. ## What happens without it Drop this cache and every leaderboard tab-open runs a fresh ZREVRANGE + 100-key MGET + JSON render. At peak, the ZSET node — which is also absorbing 50K ZADD writes/sec from ingest — would see 500K ZREVRANGEs/sec layered on top. Redis is single-threaded per shard, so writes start queueing behind reads, ingest latency spikes from 3ms to hundreds of ms, and players who just finished matches see their scores take 10+ seconds to appear. Operators see one saturated Redis node; users see a frozen leaderboard. ## The number Peak read load is **~500K req/sec**. With a 1-second TTL on `lb:global:top100`, the ZSET only serves ~1 rebuild per second — a **500,000× reduction** in ZREVRANGE load. The other 499,999 requests never touch the skiplist. ## Trade-off Players can see a leaderboard up to ~1 second stale — which is why the WebSocket push exists for the cases where that actually matters.

snap.name: Snapshot / Batch Job
snap.summary: Periodic reconciler that rebuilds Redis ZSETs from the durable DB and writes hourly snapshots for disaster recovery.

sections.heading: Trigger cadence
sections.body:
- Hourly: snapshot current ZSET to S3 (dump + compress) for point-in-time recovery
- Nightly: full rebuild of the ZSET from `best_scores` — catches any drift from async DB writes
- On-demand: after Redis failover, the warm replica serves reads while the rebuild runs in the background

sections.heading: Rebuild algorithm
sections.body:
```
# Pipelined ZADD to avoid 100M round trips
pipe = redis.pipeline
for row in db.select_streaming("SELECT user_id, best_score FROM best_scores WHERE game_mode='global'"): pipe.zadd("leaderboard:global", {row.user_id: row.best_score}) if pipe.cmd_count >= 5000: pipe.execute pipe = redis.pipeline
pipe.execute
```
~100M rows at 5K/batch, ~500ms/batch → rebuild finishes in ~10 min per shard.

sections.heading: Season rollover
sections.body: At season end, the job snapshots the final board, archives it to S3, and TRUNCATEs `leaderboard:season:N` — new season starts with an empty ZSET.

bottlenecks.title: Nightly full rebuild read-lock contention starves live ingest
bottlenecks.trigger: Nightly rebuild streams 100M rows from best_scores (SELECT... WHERE game_mode='global') while the DB primary is concurrently absorbing ~50K INSERT/sec and 50K best_scores UPSERT/sec from ingest. A 10-min full table scan competes for buffer cache and issues long-running snapshot transactions that pin dead tuples and block autovacuum. If the rebuild runs during a regional tournament window (tournaments aren't uniformly at night globally), best_scores UPSERTs block on row-level locks held by the streaming read's MVCC snapshot.
bottlenecks.symptom: During rebuild, ingest WAL backlog grows (wal_pending_rows climbing on every replica), best_scores UPSERT p99 jumps from 5ms to 200ms+, DB buffer cache hit ratio drops below 90%, autovacuum on scores falls further behind, and the rebuild itself takes 30+ min instead of 10. On-call sees correlated latency spikes on /v1/scores POST exactly when the snap job is running.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run the streaming SELECT against a read replica (not the primary) with a dedicated 'reporting' replica sized for the scan. Use server-side cursors with FETCH 5000 to bound memory and snapshot age. Schedule rebuilds per-region during that region's off-peak (not a single global 'night'). Add a CDC-driven incremental reconciler (Debezium tailing best_scores.updated_at) so the nightly full rebuild becomes a weekly verification instead of a daily requirement.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on snap_rebuild_duration_s > 900 (1.5x baseline), db_replica_lag_bytes > 1 GB during rebuild window, and correlation between snap_job_active=1 and ingest_p99_latency_ms > 30ms. Track pg_stat_activity for snapshot transactions older than 5 min during rebuild.

bottlenecks.title: Pipelined ZADD rebuild saturates Redis single-threaded event loop
bottlenecks.trigger: Rebuild pipelines ZADDs at 5000/batch against the same ZSET primary that's serving live traffic: 50K ZADD GT/sec from ingest + ~100K ZREVRANGE/ZREVRANK/sec from read cache misses and user-rank queries. Adding ~170K rebuild ZADDs/sec (100M rows / 600s) on a single-threaded Redis shard pushes ops/sec past the ~200K ceiling identified for the ZSET, with the rebuild taking cache lines cold and competing for the event loop.
bottlenecks.symptom: During rebuild: ingest ZADD p99 latency spikes from 1ms to 30–100ms, read API cache-miss ZREVRANGE latency jumps to 20ms+, Redis INFO shows instantaneous_ops_per_sec pegged near 250K, slowlog fills with ZADD entries from the rebuild pipeline, and the leaderboard visibly 'freezes' (1s cache TTL starts missing consistently). WS rank_change fan-out lags 2–5 seconds.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run rebuilds against a separate Redis instance (shadow ZSET), then atomically swap via RENAME once complete — live traffic never sees the rebuild writes. Alternatively throttle pipeline cadence (e.g. 1000 ops/batch with 5ms sleep between batches) to cap rebuild load at <20% of shard capacity. During Redis failover, accept that the warm replica serves stale reads while a full rebuild runs on a fresh primary rather than rebuilding in-place.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on redis_instantaneous_ops_per_sec > 180K during snap_job_active=1, zadd_p99_latency_ms > 10ms, and cache_miss_rate on lb:global:top100 > 1% correlated with rebuild windows. Track rebuild_ops_per_sec as a separate metric and enforce a budget (e.g. <30K/sec).

bottlenecks.title: Hourly S3 snapshot fork/BGSAVE OOM at 8 GB ZSET + tournament write load
bottlenecks.trigger: Hourly snapshot dumps the ZSET to S3 via BGSAVE (or DUMP + stream). BGSAVE forks the Redis process; copy-on-write means RSS can double during the snapshot when write rate is high. At 8 GB ZSET (global alone; 56 GB across all scopes if co-located) and 50K ZADD/sec during tournaments, COW page-touch rate is ~200 MB/sec, so a 30s BGSAVE dirties ~6 GB — pushing a 16 GB node past maxmemory and triggering OOM-kill. Snapshot uploads to S3 are ~1 GB compressed; at 50 MB/sec egress the upload takes 20s, during which a second hourly trigger could overlap.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis rdb_last_bgsave_status flips to 'err', used_memory_rss approaches maxmemory, mem_fragmentation_ratio > 1.8, and occasionally the Redis process is OOM-killed mid-tournament causing a Sentinel failover (3s ingest outage + 50K lost ZADDs per the AOF bottleneck). S3 snapshot objects show gaps in the hourly cadence; DR exercise finds the most recent recoverable snapshot is 4+ hours old.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use Redis replication to a dedicated 'snapshot replica' and run BGSAVE only on that replica — primary never forks. Set maxmemory to 50% of RAM (not 75%) to guarantee fork headroom. Enable diskless replication (`repl-diskless-sync yes`) for the snapshot stream. Stagger hourly triggers per-shard with ±5 min jitter so multi-shard clusters don't fork simultaneously. Verify S3 snapshot integrity with a checksum recorded in a metadata table and alert on missing hourly objects.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on rdb_last_bgsave_status!= 'ok', rdb_last_bgsave_time_sec > 60, and used_memory_peak / maxmemory > 0.85 during BGSAVE. S3 lifecycle check: alert if no new snapshot object appears within 75 min of the previous one. Track fork_time_ms and latest_fork_usec — anything >500ms blocks the event loop and is visible as ingest latency.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Snapshot Job is here For this leaderboard, **Redis is fast but forgetful**. The ZSET holding all 100M player ranks lives in memory on a Redis node, and the ingest path writes to Redis *first*, then asynchronously flushes to the durable SQL database in 50-row batches. That means at any given moment, Redis and the DB can disagree — Redis might have a score the DB hasn't persisted yet, or (worse) the DB has scores that never made it back into Redis after a failover. The snapshot job is the **reconciler** that periodically rebuilds the ZSET from the `best_scores` table so the two stores don't drift forever, and it also dumps hourly backups to S3 so you can recover from a total Redis loss. ## What happens without it Imagine Redis crashes mid-tournament and the replica's AOF is 30 seconds behind. Without the snapshot job, when a fresh Redis comes up, the ZSET is *empty* — every player's rank is gone. Users open the app and see a blank leaderboard or, worse, yesterday's stale ranks because no component knows how to repopulate memory from the DB. Support gets flooded ("I was #42, now I'm unranked!") and operators have no automated path back to a correct state. ## The number The ZSET holds **100M entries**. A pipelined rebuild at 5,000 ZADDs per batch, ~500ms per batch, means 100,000,000 / 5,000 × 0.5s ≈ **10,000 seconds… no, ~10 minutes** per full rebuild. That's short enough to run nightly without disrupting live traffic, but only because the ZSET's skiplist accepts sorted inserts cheaply. ## Trade-off The designer accepted that Redis and the DB can diverge for up to an hour between reconciliations — fine for a game, fatal for a payments ledger.

ws.name: WebSocket Push
ws.summary: Long-lived WebSocket server fanning out rank-change events to subscribed clients during live tournaments.

sections.heading: Subscription model
sections.body: Client opens a WS and sends `{"sub":"lb:global:top100"}` or `{"sub":"lb:user:u_18232:window"}`. Server keeps a map {subscription → [conn_ids]} and fans events out from the ingest API.

sections.heading: Event filter
sections.body:
Not every score submission triggers a push. Only fire when:
- New score enters the top-100 (ZREVRANK < 100)
- A user's own window would visibly change (rank ± 5 affected)
This cuts WS traffic by 100x during non-tournament idle.

sections.heading: Scaling
sections.body: Sharded by user_id hash. 1M concurrent connections ≈ 20 nodes at 50K conns/node (typical for tuned Netty/Go). Heartbeat every 30s to detect dead conns.

bottlenecks.title: Fan-out amplification on top-100 subscribers during tournament
bottlenecks.trigger: During a live tournament, ~100K active viewers subscribe to lb:global:top100 while ingest runs at 50K submissions/sec. Even if only ~0.1% of submissions actually cross the top-100 boundary (~50/sec), each such event fans out to all 100K subscribers = 5M WS frames/sec across the 20-node fleet = 250K frames/sec/node. A tournament-finale rally with a top-of-table battle can push boundary-crossing events to 500/sec, yielding 50M frames/sec fleetwide.
bottlenecks.symptom: WS node CPU pegs at 100% on serialization+send syscalls; event queue depth grows with publish_to_deliver latency climbing from ~10ms to 2–10s; clients see the live ticker stall then dump a burst of stale updates; TCP send buffers fill and kernel back-pressures the app with EAGAIN; some connections get dropped when per-conn outbound buffer exceeds limit.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Coalesce events at the publisher: batch rank changes into 200ms windows and send one delta frame containing all top-100 mutations instead of N separate frames. Pre-serialize the broadcast payload once per event and use writev/sendmmsg to share the buffer across connections (zero-copy per-subscriber). Shard top-100 subscriptions across dedicated 'broadcast' WS nodes separate from per-user-window nodes so fan-out load doesn't crush narrow-subscription traffic. Drop-oldest policy on per-conn queue >100 pending frames.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on ws_publish_to_deliver_p99_ms > 500, ws_outbound_frames_per_sec_per_node > 150K, per_conn_send_buffer_bytes p99 > 256KB, and ws_dropped_frames_rate > 0. Track (boundary_events_per_sec × top100_subscribers) as a predictive load metric.

bottlenecks.title: Reconnect storm on mobile network churn at 1M concurrent
bottlenecks.trigger: 1M concurrent WS connections across 20 nodes = 50K conns/node. Mobile NAT timeouts (30–300s) and wifi↔LTE transitions produce ~1% reconnect/min = 10K reconnects/sec fleetwide = 500/sec/node. Each reconnect requires TLS handshake + auth + subscription restore + initial state replay (top-100 snapshot = ~14KB). At worst-case correlated churn (cell tower flap, ISP blip), 5–10% of conns reconnect within 10s = 50–100K new conns/sec fleetwide.
bottlenecks.symptom: WS node CPU spikes from steady-state ~40% to 95%+; new upgrades queue behind handshakes; existing subscribers see their event stream pause for seconds while the node serves reconnect work; LB reports ws_upgrade_p99 > 2s; subscribers_gauge shows correlated dip-then-recover pattern; memory growth on resubscribe-state structures.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Issue a resume_token (session_id + last_seq) at subscribe time so reconnects skip full state replay and only get events since last_seq from a 60s ring buffer. Client-side exponential backoff with jitter (base 500ms, cap 10s) and SO_KEEPALIVE 25s to avoid mid-NAT death. Dedicated reconnect-handling path on the WS node with lower priority than steady-state sends. Fall back to 2s short-poll /v1/leaderboard/global when WS unhealthy so the WS fleet doesn't become a single point of leaderboard liveness.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on ws_reconnects_per_sec > 5K fleetwide or > 500/node sustained 1 min, ws_upgrade_p99_ms > 1000, resume_token_miss_rate > 20% (indicates ring buffer too small), and subscribers_gauge drop > 20% in 60s.

bottlenecks.title: Subscription index lookup cost on every ingest rank change
bottlenecks.trigger: Every CH=1 ZADD from ingest (~50K/sec peak, but after dedup ~5–10K/sec produce actual rank changes in any subscribed window) requires the publisher to compute subscribers_overlapping(old_rank, ±5) ∪ subscribers_overlapping(new_rank, ±5). With 100K neighborhood subscribers spread over 100M ranks, a naive scan is cheap but a correct index (rank-bucketed subscription map) must be maintained as every user's own rank drifts. At 50K ZADDs/sec × 2 lookups/event, that's 100K index probes/sec plus index updates when subscribers themselves change rank.
bottlenecks.symptom: Publisher-side CPU on WS coordination nodes grows linearly with ingest QPS; event emission latency (ingest→WS fanout) p99 creeps from 10ms to 100ms+; memory for subscription-by-rank index grows unpredictably as ranks shift; stale index entries cause missed pushes (user subscribed to own window but event goes to old bucket).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Key subscriptions by user_id instead of rank — on each rank_change event, look up only the caller's own subscription plus fixed subscribers of predefined boards (top100, region boards) — O(1) per event. Let the client re-request its window on any received event rather than server-computing overlap. Maintain subscription index in a Redis hash sharded by user_id hash, with TTL matching WS connection lifetime so stale entries self-clean.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on ws_event_dispatch_p99_ms > 50, subscription_index_size_bytes growth rate > 10MB/min, missed_push_audit_rate > 0.01% (sampled reconciliation: did user_id with an active subscription get the event?), and cpu_on_coordinator_nodes > 60% during steady-state ingest.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why WebSocket Push is here For a real-time gaming leaderboard, the word that matters is **real-time**. During a tournament, players staring at the top-100 expect to see ranks shuffle *as scores come in* — not after they pull-to-refresh. The rest of the system (Redis ZSET, cached top-100 blob, read API) is built for **pull**: clients ask, server answers. That works fine for someone casually opening the Leaderboard tab, but it's wrong for the 100K viewers watching a finale. Polling `/v1/leaderboard/global` every second from 100K clients would add 100K QPS of pure noise on top of the 500K peak reads — most of those polls return identical bytes. WebSocket Push inverts the flow: the server already knows when a rank changed (ingest just did the ZADD), so it tells only the clients who care. ## What happens without it Drop the WS tier and tournament UX collapses into one of two bad shapes. Either clients poll aggressively (say every 500ms) and you've just doubled your read fleet and cache bandwidth for data that barely changed, or they poll lazily (every 5s) and the leaderboard feels *dead* — a player finishes a match, sees "New rank: 4321", switches to the board, and their own row hasn't updated yet. Operators see a flat, wasteful read-QPS graph; users see a laggy ticker and complain the game "lies" about ranks. ## The number Capacity estimates **1M concurrent players × 10% actively viewing during a tournament ≈ 100K live subscribers**. At ~20 WS nodes that's 50K connections/node — tractable. If those same 100K users polled once per second instead, that's 100K extra QPS on the read path, roughly a **20% blow-up** of peak read load for information the server already has in hand. ## Trade-off Long-lived connections bring operational pain (reconnect storms, NAT timeouts, per-conn memory), which is why the design gates WS behind a conditional fan-out — only fire when top-100 or a watched neighborhood actually changed.

operations.title: Submit score (ZADD + persist + conditional push)
operations.name: Submit score (ZADD + persist + conditional push)
operations.description: Player finishes a match. Client signs and POSTs the score. API verifies, writes to Redis ZSET and durable DB, and emits a WebSocket event if the rank actually changed inside a watched window.

steps.title: Player finishes a ranked match
steps.action: Client computes the final score, signs it with the session key, and POSTs to /v1/scores. The score endpoint is idempotent on (user_id, match_id) so client retries are safe.
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST /v1/scores HTTP/1.1
Host: api.game.com
Authorization: Bearer <session_token>
Content-Type: application/json { "user_id": "u_18232", "game_mode": "ranked_duel", "score": 42815, "match_id": "m_8f12a9", "region": "us-west", "client_sig": "hmac_sha256:4f3c9e..."
}

steps.title: LB routes /v1/scores to ingest fleet
steps.action: Path prefix /v1/scores maps to the ingest backend pool. Least-connections across healthy ingest replicas.
steps.codeOrCommand:
pool = routes["/v1/scores"] # ingest-pool
upstream = pool.pick(algo="least_conn", healthy=True)
forward(req → upstream)

steps.title: Ingest verifies signature and dedupes on match_id
steps.action: Ingest API recomputes the HMAC with the server-side session key and compares with client_sig. Looks up (user_id, match_id) in a small local Bloom filter of recent submissions to reject replays without hitting the DB.
steps.codeOrCommand:
expected = hmac_sha256(session_key["u_18232"], f"{match_id}|{score}|{nonce}")
if expected!= req.client_sig: return 403 InvalidSignature if recent_dedup_bloom.might_contain(("u_18232","m_8f12a9")): if db.exists_score("u_18232","m_8f12a9"): return 200 {"status":"duplicate"} # idempotent recent_dedup_bloom.add(("u_18232","m_8f12a9"))

steps.title: Redis ZADD GT updates the global board
steps.action: Redis ZADD with GT flag only updates if the new score exceeds the stored one; CH returns the number of changed elements. Skiplist insert/reorder is O(log N) ≈ 27 hops at N=100M.
steps.codeOrCommand:
ZADD leaderboard:global GT u_18232
# internally: skiplist.find("u_18232") → prev_score=39210
# 42815 > 39210 → remove old node, insert at new rank, fix skiplist pointers
# returns: (integer) 1 (CH = 1 element changed) ZADD leaderboard:region:us-west GT u_18232
ZADD leaderboard:mode:ranked_duel GT u_18232
steps.decision: CH=1 → score actually improved, proceed to push + DB persist. If CH=0 (old score >= new score), we'd skip the WS push but still persist to DB for audit.

steps.title: Ingest writes row to scores DB (async)
steps.action: Fire-and-forget from the API's perspective: the row is appended to a local WAL on the ingest replica and flushed to the DB in 50-row batches every ~50ms. Client response does not wait for this.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Local WAL append (sub-ms)
wal.append({ "user_id": "u_18232", "match_id": "m_8f12a9", "game_mode": "ranked_duel", "region": "us-west", "score": 42815, "submitted_at": "2026-04-24T10:17:11Z"
})
# Batch flusher (every ~50ms, 50 rows per flush):
INSERT INTO scores (user_id, match_id, game_mode, region, score, submitted_at)
VALUES ('u_18232','m_8f12a9','ranked_duel','us-west',42815,'2026-04-24T10:17:11Z'),...
ON CONFLICT (user_id, match_id) DO NOTHING; -- And maintain best_scores:
INSERT INTO best_scores (user_id, game_mode, region, best_score, updated_at)
VALUES ('u_18232','ranked_duel','us-west',42815, now)
ON CONFLICT (user_id, game_mode) DO UPDATE SET best_score = GREATEST(best_scores.best_score, EXCLUDED.best_score), updated_at = now;
steps.note: Async DB write tolerates 30s of DB downtime via the WAL. On crash before flush, <30s of scores are lost — acceptable for a game leaderboard (not a bank).

steps.title: WebSocket push to subscribers (conditional)
steps.action: Check whether this rank change is user-visible: inside top-100, or inside any subscribed user's ±5 window. If yes, fan out a compact event to just those WS connections.
steps.codeOrCommand: if new_rank < 100 or old_rank < 100: # top-100 boundary may have shifted fanout("lb:global:top100", { "event": "rank_change", "user_id": "u_18232", "new_rank": 4321, "score": 42815 }) for sub in subscribers_overlapping(4321, window=5) | subscribers_overlapping(9182, window=5): conn.send(sub.conn_id, { "event": "rank_change", "user_id": "u_18232", "new_rank": 4321 })
steps.decision: new_rank=4321 is outside top-100, so no top-100 broadcast — only the 31 users whose ±5 window contains the old or new rank get a frame. Saves ~8400 unnecessary broadcasts per submission during non-tournament.

steps.title: Ingest returns 202 Accepted to client
steps.action: API responds as soon as ZADD commits — DB flush and WS fan-out run in parallel and do not block the response.

steps.title: LB relays response
steps.action: Return path through the LB.

steps.title: Client updates local UI
steps.action: Client shows the 'New rank: 4321' confetti animation. End-to-end submit latency typically 15–40ms.

operations.title: Read top-100 leaderboard (ZREVRANGE, cached)
operations.name: Read top-100 leaderboard (ZREVRANGE, cached)
operations.description: User opens the leaderboard tab. Read API serves from a 1s-TTL cache; on miss it issues a ZREVRANGE and hydrates display names.

steps.title: User taps 'Leaderboard' tab
steps.action: Client requests the top-100 global board. Optimistically renders last known list while the request is in-flight.

steps.title: LB routes to read fleet
steps.action: Prefix /v1/leaderboard/* maps to the read backend pool — separated from ingest so a write storm doesn't starve readers.

steps.title: Read API checks response cache
steps.action: Single Redis GET on the pre-rendered top-100 JSON. Hit rate is near 100% during steady state because the TTL (1s) is shorter than the read interval (~10ms between requests at 500K QPS).
steps.codeOrCommand:
blob = cache.get("lb:global:top100")
if blob is not None: return Response(200, json=blob) # cache HIT
# else: request coalescing — first miss fetches, others wait on a short-lived semaphore

steps.title: Redis cache returns rendered blob (HIT)
steps.action: O(1) hash lookup; sub-millisecond. Blob is already serialized JSON — no CPU to re-render.

steps.title: Read API returns 200 OK
steps.action: Response body is the cached JSON verbatim plus a Cache-Control: max-age=1 header so clients themselves throttle repeat calls.

steps.title: LB relays response
steps.action: Return path.

steps.title: Client renders top-100 list
steps.action: Hot-path latency typically 5–15ms. During cache-miss rebuild (TTL rollover), read API issues a ZREVRANGE against the ZSET — same flow but with an extra hop described below.

steps.title: [Cache MISS branch] ZREVRANGE rebuilds the blob
steps.action: When the cached blob has expired, exactly one request wins the coalescing lock and runs `ZREVRANGE leaderboard:global 0 99 WITHSCORES`. All concurrent misses wait on this one call (stampede protection).
steps.codeOrCommand:
ZREVRANGE leaderboard:global 0 99 WITHSCORES
# → [["u_441", 98214], ["u_1182", 97041], ["u_221", 96180],... 100 pairs]
# O(log N + M) = O(27 + 100) — ~1.5 ms on a hot Redis # Hydrate display names in a pipeline
MGET user:u_441:display user:u_1182:display... # 100 keys # Render JSON and write back to cache
cache.setex("lb:global:top100", 1, json.dumps(rendered))
steps.note: This branch runs at most once per second globally thanks to request coalescing — Redis sees ~1 ZREVRANGE per second, not 500K per second.

operations.title: Read user's own rank (ZREVRANK + surrounding window)
operations.name: Read user's own rank (ZREVRANK + surrounding window)
operations.description: User taps 'Where am I?'. API fetches the user's rank, then a ±5 window around it. Two Redis ops, both O(log N).

steps.title: User taps 'Where am I?'
steps.action: Client asks the server for its rank plus a surrounding window so it can render 'you are 4321 of 100M, here are your neighbors'.

steps.title: LB routes to read fleet
steps.action: Same routing as top-100 — all /v1/leaderboard/* → read pool.

steps.title: Read API fetches rank then window in a pipeline
steps.action: Two Redis ops packed into a single RTT via MULTI/pipeline: ZREVRANK to find the user's rank, then ZREVRANGE over rank-5.. rank+5.
steps.codeOrCommand:
pipe = redis.pipeline
pipe.zrevrank("leaderboard:global", "u_18232")
# We don't yet know the rank — read it, then issue the range.
rank = pipe.execute[0]
if rank is None: return 200 {"ranked": False} start = max(0, rank - 5)
stop = rank + 5
window = redis.zrevrange("leaderboard:global", start, stop, withscores=True)

steps.title: Redis: ZREVRANK u_18232 → 4321, then ZREVRANGE 4316 4326 WITHSCORES
steps.action: First op walks the skiplist to find the user and accumulate its rank (O(log N)). Second op locates rank 4316 and reads forward 11 elements (O(log N + 11)).

steps.title: Read API hydrates display names from cache
steps.action: Pipeline MGET of `user:{id}:display` for each of the 11 members. 5-minute TTL so this hits near-100% outside of name-change storms.

steps.title: Read API assembles response
steps.action: Combine the 11 (user_id, score) pairs with display names; mark the caller's own entry with `is_self: true` so the client can highlight it.

steps.title: LB relays response
steps.action: Return path.

steps.title: Client renders user card with neighbors
steps.action: End-to-end latency typically 5–10ms. Highlighted row is the caller; tapping a neighbor opens their profile.

tradeoffs.chosen: Redis ZSET (skiplist) as hot source of truth
tradeoffs.rationale: O(log N) ranked operations match the read pattern exactly; a SQL ORDER BY would force a full index scan per top-K read at 100M rows.

tradeoffs.chosen: Async dual-write to a relational scores table
tradeoffs.rationale: Keeps Redis as the fast path while ensuring no score is permanently lost if a Redis node fails. Costs a periodic snapshot job to repair drift.

tradeoffs.chosen: ZADD with GT (greater-than) and CH flags
tradeoffs.rationale: Makes retries idempotent and prevents an out-of-order replay from lowering a player's visible score. Means we rely on GT semantics being available in the client.

tradeoffs.chosen: One ZSET per logical leaderboard (global, region, tournament)
tradeoffs.rationale: Natural partition boundary and keeps each ZSET small enough to fit comfortably in one Redis instance. Global board is the only one that grows unbounded and may need further partitioning.

tradeoffs.chosen: WebSocket push only on top-K-impacting writes
tradeoffs.rationale: Keeps fan-out bounded by active viewers rather than by global write rate; the other 99% of score writes go silently to the ZSET.

interviewFollowUps.question: Shard the global ZSET across multiple Redis instances for boards beyond a single node's memory
Add a seasonal / tournament lifecycle so old ZSETs can be archived and retired
Introduce anti-cheat: server-authoritative match validation before score acceptance
Add a delta-encoded WebSocket protocol so reconnecting clients can catch up without a full replay
Expose friends-only leaderboards backed by ZINTERSTORE against a social graph key
